subject: phy
title: Dynamics
subtitle: Newton's laws, momentum, impulse and collisions.
concept: Newton's three laws describe force, acceleration and their relationship; the second law gives F = ma (for constant mass).
Momentum (p = mv) is conserved in all collisions in a closed system; impulse equals change in momentum.
Elastic collisions conserve both momentum and kinetic energy; inelastic collisions conserve only momentum.

notes.heading: Newton's Three Laws
items: First law: an object remains at rest or moves with constant velocity unless acted upon by a resultant force. This defines inertia — the resistance of an object to changes in its motion.

Second law: the resultant force on an object equals the rate of change of its momentum: F = Δp/Δt. For constant mass this simplifies to F = ma. The direction of acceleration is always in the direction of the resultant force.
Third law: if object A exerts a force on object B, then B exerts an equal and opposite force of the same type on A. Newton's third law pairs act on different objects — they never cancel each other.

notes.heading: Momentum and Impulse
items: Linear momentum p = mv (kg m s⁻¹ = N s). Momentum is a vector — direction matters.
Impulse = FΔt = Δp. Equal to the area under a force–time graph. A large force applied for a short time gives the same impulse as a smaller force applied for longer.

Conservation of momentum: in a closed system (no external resultant force), total momentum is constant before and after any interaction. This follows directly from Newton's third law — the equal and opposite forces between two objects produce equal and opposite impulses, so their combined momentum is unchanged.

notes.heading: Elastic and Inelastic Collisions
items: Elastic collision: both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved. Perfectly elastic collisions are rare in practice (hard spheres, subatomic particles).
Inelastic collision: momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy is not — some is converted to heat, sound, or deformation. Most real collisions are inelastic.
Perfectly inelastic: the objects stick together after collision. This gives the maximum possible kinetic energy loss consistent with momentum conservation.
Explosions: a system at rest has zero total momentum. After the explosion, the momenta of the fragments are equal and opposite.

definitions.body: The product of mass and velocity: p = mv; a vector quantity; SI unit kg m s⁻¹.
The product of force and the time for which it acts: impulse = FΔt = Δp; equal to the area under a force–time graph.
The total momentum of a closed system (no external forces) remains constant before and after an interaction.

workedExamples.q: A 1500 kg car travelling at 20 m s⁻¹ collides with a stationary 1000 kg car. They stick together. Find their common velocity and the KE lost.

steps.text: ½×2500×12² = 180 000 J; ΔKE = −120 000 J (lost as heat/sound)

mistakes: Applying conservation of momentum when there IS an external force (e.g. friction) — the system is not closed.
Confusing Newton's 3rd law pairs (different objects) with equilibrium forces on ONE object (1st law).
Using KE = mv² instead of ½mv².
tips: Impulse = area under F–t graph (important for variable forces).
In explosions, if total initial momentum = 0, calculate the velocity of one fragment and use conservation to find the other.
3rd law check: 'Object A pulls Object B'; 3rd law pair: 'Object B pulls Object A'. Same force type, same magnitude.

flashcards.q: State Newton's second law in terms of momentum.
flashcards.a: The resultant force equals the rate of change of momentum: F = Δp/Δt.

flashcards.q: What is impulse and what does it equal?
flashcards.a: Impulse = FΔt = change in momentum (Δp). It equals the area under a force–time graph.

flashcards.q: Distinguish between elastic and inelastic collisions.
flashcards.a: Elastic: both momentum and KE conserved. Inelastic: only momentum conserved; KE is partially converted to other forms.

flashcards.q: State the principle of conservation of momentum.
flashcards.a: Total momentum of a closed system remains constant, provided there is no resultant external force.

flashcards.q: Two ice skaters push off from rest. Skater A (60 kg) moves at 3 m s⁻¹. Find velocity of skater B (40 kg).
flashcards.a: p before = 0; 0 = 60×3 + 40×v_B; v_B = −180/40 = −4.5 m s⁻¹ (opposite direction).

flashcards.q: What is a Newton's 3rd law pair?
flashcards.a: Equal and opposite forces of the same type acting on two different objects (e.g. gravity Earth pulls you; gravity you pulls Earth).

questions.q: A 2 kg object accelerates at 5 m s⁻². What is the resultant force?
Which is conserved in ALL collisions?
questions.exp: Momentum is always conserved in a closed system; KE is only conserved in elastic collisions.

questions.q: A 5 N force acts for 3 s. What is the impulse?
questions.exp: Impulse = FΔt = 5×3 = 15 N s (= 15 kg m s⁻¹).

questions.q: Two 1 kg balls collide head-on: ball 1 at +5 m s⁻¹, ball 2 at −3 m s⁻¹. What is total momentum before?
Identify the correct Newton's 3rd law pair for 'Earth pulls the Moon (gravity)':
opts: Moon's weight and Moon's normal contact force
questions.exp: 3rd law pair: same force type (gravity), same magnitude, opposite direction, on DIFFERENT objects — Moon pulls Earth gravitationally.

recall: State Newton's three laws of motion.
Define momentum and state its SI units.
Apply conservation of momentum to collisions and explosions.
Distinguish between elastic and inelastic collisions.
Explain why momentum is conserved using Newton's laws.
